The sailor later recovers the animal, Le Bon is released, and Dupin has solved the case by explaining evidence the police treated as contradictions.

characters.description: An English army officer invalided home from the Western Front, recovering on sick leave when an old friend invites him to convalesce at Styles Court. Amiable, conventional, and rather too ready to be impressed by whoever he has spoken to last, he has a private ambition to try his hand at detection. He narrates the case, recording what he sees and what he is told, and he is often several steps behind the man he brings into it.
characters.name: Arthur Hastings

characters.description: A retired Belgian police detective, small, precise, and elaborately moustached, living in the nearby village among a party of war refugees whose settlement Mrs Inglethorp has paid for. He limps a little and dresses with fastidious care, insists on order in small things, and prefers to sit and reason from the arrangement of a room rather than crawl about measuring footprints. Hastings knew him years earlier in Belgium and holds his abilities in high regard.
characters.name: Hercule Poirot

characters.description: The elderly mistress of Styles Court in Essex, an energetic and autocratic woman who controls the money that keeps the household and much of the district going. She sits on committees, organises war charities, and expects gratitude. The estate came to her from her first husband, and her stepsons live on her allowance rather than on any inheritance of their own. She has recently married a much younger man, to the dismay of her family.
characters.name: Emily Inglethorp

characters.description: Mrs Inglethorp's new husband, some twenty years her junior, with a long black beard, thick spectacles, and a stiff, ceremonious manner. He is a distant relation of her companion, appeared in the district only recently, and is universally assumed by the household and the village to have married for money. He takes charge of his wife's affairs and is disliked by every member of the family.
characters.name: Alfred Inglethorp

characters.description: Mrs Inglethorp's elder stepson and Hastings's friend, who invites him to Styles. A country magistrate of middle age, he farms a little, keeps up appearances on an allowance from his stepmother, and resents both his dependence and her new marriage. His own marriage is visibly cool, and there is village talk of his attentions to a farmer's young wife.
characters.name: John Cavendish

characters.description: John Cavendish's wife, striking and reserved, with a stillness that Hastings finds difficult to read. She keeps her own counsel, moves about the grounds alone, and is on distant terms with her husband. She is on friendlier terms with a London specialist staying in the village, which the household notices.
characters.name: Mary Cavendish

characters.description: The younger Cavendish brother, a qualified doctor who never practised and now writes indifferent verse. Diffident, moody, and easily flustered, he lives at Styles on the same allowance as his brother. He is fond of the young dispenser who lodges with the family and worries about her more than he admits.
characters.name: Lawrence Cavendish

characters.description: Mrs Inglethorp's companion and factotum for some years, a large, weather-beaten, plain-spoken woman who runs errands, gardens, and manages the household's practical business. She is devoted to her employer and states her opinions without softening them, chief among them that the new husband is a fortune hunter. Her insistence on saying so provokes a quarrel that drives her from the house.
characters.name: Evelyn Howard

characters.description: A young woman without means whom Mrs Inglethorp has taken in as a protegee. Cheerful and lively, she works at the dispensary of the local Red Cross hospital, where she makes up prescriptions and has ready access to the poisons cupboard. Hastings admires her considerably.
characters.name: Cynthia Murdoch

characters.description: A distinguished London specialist in toxicology, staying in the village ostensibly to rest after a breakdown in health. Dark, saturnine, and formal, he is a frequent visitor at Styles, where he is on notably good terms with Mary Cavendish. He is given to long solitary walks at night, which the neighbourhood finds odd in a convalescent.
characters.name: Dr Bauerstein

characters.description: The elderly parlourmaid at Styles, long in Mrs Inglethorp's service and loyal to her. She carries the household's coffee and cocoa, knows the routine of the bedrooms, and overhears a quarrel in the boudoir on the afternoon before the tragedy. Her account of times and small domestic details becomes important evidence.
characters.name: Dorcas

characters.description: A Scotland Yard detective inspector, brisk and cheerful, who has worked with Poirot on Continental cases and treats him with amused respect. He is sent down to Styles once the death becomes a police matter and is prepared to act on the evidence in front of him.
characters.name: Inspector Japp

recaps.ending: Poirot recovers the missing letter, which had been rolled up and pushed into an ornamental spill vase on the mantelpiece of the boudoir. It proves that Alfred Inglethorp and Evelyn Howard are secretly cousins and lovers who planned the murder together. Miss Howard's loudly advertised hatred of him was cover; it was she, disguised with a false beard and glasses, who bought strychnine at the village chemist's and signed his name, so that the evidence pointing at him could be demolished at will. The poison was worked into Mrs Inglethorp's bromide sleeping powders, so that her medicine delivered a concentrated fatal dose days later, with both of them apparently elsewhere. Alfred courted suspicion deliberately, planning to produce an unshakeable alibi at his trial and be acquitted beyond any second prosecution. Poirot's refusal to let him be arrested too early is what makes the case against him possible. The pair are taken into custody. John Cavendish is acquitted and reconciles with Mary, whose coldness had been jealousy rather than indifference. Lawrence Cavendish and Cynthia Murdoch become engaged, Hastings having proposed to Cynthia himself and been gently refused. Dr Bauerstein's night walks are explained by his arrest as an enemy agent, unconnected with the murder. Hastings leaves Styles with his admiration for Poirot confirmed, and the two agree to work together again.
recaps.in_short: Invalided home from the war, Captain Hastings goes to stay at Styles Court, where his friend John Cavendish lives on the money of his elderly stepmother, Emily Inglethorp, who has just married a much younger man the whole family distrusts. Mrs Inglethorp dies in the night of strychnine poisoning behind a bolted door, hours after a violent quarrel and after making and apparently destroying a new will. Hastings brings in Hercule Poirot, a Belgian detective living among refugees in the village. Suspicion falls on the husband, but Poirot works to protect him, then dismantles the case against him in public. Instead the family closes in: John Cavendish is arrested and tried. Poirot finds the letter everyone has been looking for hidden in a vase, and shows that Alfred Inglethorp and Evelyn Howard, secretly cousins and lovers, poisoned Mrs Inglethorp between them, using her own sleeping powders to delay the dose and inviting suspicion that could be safely destroyed later. John is acquitted, and the guilty pair are arrested.

recaps.text: Captain Hastings, on sick leave from the Front, accepts an invitation from his friend John Cavendish to convalesce at Styles Court in Essex. The house belongs to John's stepmother, Emily Inglethorp, a wealthy and managing old lady on whose allowance the family lives. She has recently married Alfred Inglethorp, a bearded man twenty years her junior whom the entire household believes to be after her money. Also at Styles are John's reserved wife Mary, his diffident brother Lawrence, Cynthia Murdoch, a young dependant who works in a hospital dispensary, and Evelyn Howard, Mrs Inglethorp's blunt and devoted companion. Miss Howard says openly that Mr Inglethorp is a fortune hunter, quarrels with her employer over it, and leaves the house. In the village Hastings meets an old acquaintance, Hercule Poirot, a retired Belgian detective living among refugees whose lodging Mrs Inglethorp pays for. Tension in the house grows; on the afternoon of the 17th of July Mrs Inglethorp is heard quarrelling violently with someone in her boudoir, drives into town, and returns tired and secretive, taking her papers to bed with her.

In the small hours the household is woken by Mrs Inglethorp in convulsions behind her locked bedroom door. The doors to the adjoining rooms are bolted as well and have to be forced. She dies before the doctors can do anything, and Dr Bauerstein, a London toxicologist staying in the village, says at once that the symptoms are those of strychnine. Her husband is not in the house. Hastings walks to the village and asks Poirot to take the case; Poirot agrees on condition that he is allowed to pursue it to the end in his own way. Examining the sealed bedroom he notes a coffee cup ground to powder in the grate's fender, a small stain on the carpet, an overturned table, a scrap of dark green fabric caught on the bolt of the door into Cynthia's room, and, in the fireplace, a charred fragment of a will made that very afternoon. The despatch case in which Mrs Inglethorp kept her private papers has been forced open and something taken from it. Poirot learns that she had summoned her solicitor and made a new will only hours before she died.

Analysis confirms strychnine, and the question becomes how it was administered, since the coffee and the cocoa she drank both test clear and the poison acted far later in the night than it should have. At the inquest the evidence turns against Alfred Inglethorp: a chemist's assistant testifies that he sold strychnine to a man he took to be Mr Inglethorp, who signed the poison book in that name; the destroyed will was believed to have been in his favour; and he flatly refuses to say where he spent the evening of the murder. Miss Howard is recalled and repeats her opinion with force. The coroner's jury returns wilful murder against a person or persons unknown, but the village and the police are in no doubt. Hastings expects Poirot to hand the man over. Instead Poirot announces that his object is to prevent Alfred Inglethorp's arrest, and will not explain why.

When the police are ready to make the arrest, Poirot forces the issue in front of Inspector Japp of Scotland Yard: he demonstrates that Inglethorp can account for the crucial evening with witnesses who cannot be shaken, and that the chemist's evidence therefore proves only that somebody impersonated him. A false black beard is found in the attic dressing-up chest, recently used. Attention swings back to the household. Poirot pursues small things that nobody else considers evidence: the shred of green fabric, an extra coffee cup that has vanished, the papers taken from the despatch case, Lawrence Cavendish's white face in the sickroom, and Mary Cavendish's movements in the night. Dr Bauerstein's habit of tramping the countryside after dark, and his friendship with Mary, attract suspicion of their own. Relations between John and Mary Cavendish deteriorate to open estrangement.

Dr Bauerstein is arrested, but for espionage rather than murder; his night walks had nothing to do with the poisoning. Then the police act on the evidence they have assembled and arrest John Cavendish, whose quarrel with his stepmother, chronic need of money and unexplained purchase of a false beard tell heavily against him. He is committed for trial. Mary, shaken out of her reserve, admits to Hastings that she was in her mother-in-law's room that night and that the torn green fabric was hers; she had gone in hoping to find a document of her own concern. Poirot, who could have destroyed the prosecution's case at once, holds back, telling Hastings only that a single missing link would make everything certain. The trial goes badly. Counsel for the defence can shake nothing, and the verdict looks a foregone conclusion.

Poirot finds the missing link: the letter taken from the despatch case, rolled up and hidden in a spill vase on the boudoir mantelpiece, where nobody had thought to look. It is a note from Alfred Inglethorp to Evelyn Howard, and it proves that the two are secretly cousins and lovers who planned the murder together. Miss Howard's public loathing of him was a blind. She bought the strychnine in the village disguised in a false beard and glasses, signing his name so that the evidence against him would be certain to collapse; Alfred deliberately refused to explain his movements, intending to be tried, acquitted, and so put beyond a second prosecution. The strychnine was added to Mrs Inglethorp's bromide sleeping powders, so that her tonic delivered a concentrated dose days later, at an hour when both of them could show they were elsewhere. Poirot's obstruction of the early arrest is what makes the true case possible. The pair are taken. John Cavendish is acquitted and reconciled with Mary; Lawrence, who had suppressed evidence in the belief that Cynthia was implicated, becomes engaged to her; and Hastings, refused by Cynthia, leaves Styles with his faith in Poirot complete.

characters.description: A retired Belgian detective travelling to the Riviera on the Blue Train. He has no official position in the case, but Rufus Van Aldin asks for his help and the French police are willing to work with him. He studies the passengers' relationships and prepared stories as closely as the physical evidence.
characters.name: Hercule Poirot

characters.description: A sensible young Englishwoman who has spent years as the paid companion of an exacting old lady in St Mary Mead. A legacy unexpectedly makes her wealthy and independent, leaving her free to travel and decide what kind of life she wants after years spent arranging someone else's.
characters.name: Katherine Grey

characters.description: An American financier who built a vast fortune through force, calculation, and a refusal to lose. He is devoted to his daughter Ruth and deeply distrustful of both her estranged husband and the French aristocrat she has been seeing. He gives her a celebrated ruby called the Heart of Fire before she leaves for the Riviera.
characters.name: Rufus Van Aldin

characters.description: Rufus Van Aldin's daughter, rich, unhappy, and separated from her husband Derek. She has resumed an entanglement with the Comte de la Roche despite her father's warnings, and boards the Blue Train intending to meet the count in Paris while carrying the Heart of Fire among her jewels.
characters.name: Ruth Kettering

characters.description: Ruth's estranged English husband, handsome, charming, and chronically short of money. Van Aldin regards him as an adventurer and is pressing Ruth to divorce him. Derek is also involved with the dancer Mirelle, though neither money nor affection has made that relationship simple.
characters.name: Derek Kettering

characters.description: Van Aldin's British secretary, a former army major whose war wound ended his service. Quiet, capable, and trusted with his employer's most private business, he manages sensitive arrangements with tact and efficiency.
characters.name: Major Richard Knighton

characters.description: Ruth Kettering's personal maid, travelling in the adjoining compartment. She reports that her mistress dismissed her for the night in Paris and that a man was present in Ruth's compartment, though she says she could not see his face.
characters.name: Ada Mason

characters.description: A polished French aristocrat with a taste for wealthy women and valuable objects. Ruth has been drawn back to him while separated from Derek, and her father believes the count is interested chiefly in the ruby she carries.
characters.name: Comte Armand de la Roche

characters.description: A celebrated dancer and Derek Kettering's lover, passionate, possessive, and accustomed to turning every entrance into a performance. She is certain Derek will soon be free to marry her and speaks of their future as settled.
characters.name: Mirelle

characters.description: Katherine's wealthy cousin, an invalid who presides over a fashionable and financially strained household on the Riviera. She invites Katherine to stay at the Villa Marguerite and watches the investigation with lively curiosity.
characters.name: Lady Rosalie Tamplin

characters.description: Rosalie Tamplin's forthright daughter, much younger in manner and considerably more perceptive than the rest of the villa's social circle. She takes a protective interest in Katherine and is candid about Derek Kettering.
characters.name: Lenox Tamplin

characters.description: A Paris dealer whose knowledge extends beyond respectable antiques. Poirot has dealt with him before and consults him about the history of the Heart of Fire and the international jewel thief known as the Marquis.
characters.name: Demetrius Papopolous

recaps.ending: Poirot identifies Major Richard Knighton as both Ruth Kettering's murderer and the elusive jewel thief known as the Marquis. Knighton's trusted position gave him full knowledge of Van Aldin's gift and Ruth's travel plans. Ada Mason was his accomplice: her account of seeing a man in Ruth's compartment was designed to point toward the Comte de la Roche, and her description could be adjusted as the investigation required. Knighton killed Ruth on the train and took the Heart of Fire, while the count's planned meeting and Derek's presence supplied convenient alternative suspects. Poirot uses Papopolous's knowledge of the jewel trade, Knighton's handling of evidence, and pressure on Mason to break the prepared story. The ruby is recovered and the count's fraud exposed, though he is not the killer. Derek is cleared of Ruth's murder. Mirelle's attempt to hold him with incriminating claims fails, and his attachment to Katherine becomes plain. Knighton's courtship of Katherine is revealed as part concealment and part miscalculation; Katherine survives the case and is free to choose a future with Derek.
recaps.in_short: Rufus Van Aldin gives his estranged daughter Ruth Kettering the Heart of Fire, a famous ruby, before she takes the Blue Train to the Riviera. Ruth plans to meet her lover, the Comte de la Roche, while her impecunious husband Derek and the dancer Mirelle complicate her private life. On the journey Ruth befriends Katherine Grey, newly wealthy after years as a companion. Ruth is found murdered in her compartment and the ruby is gone. Poirot investigates at Van Aldin's request, testing the evidence of Ruth's maid Ada Mason, the count's schemes, Derek's movements, and Mirelle's jealousy. He discovers that Van Aldin's trusted secretary, Major Richard Knighton, is the international thief known as the Marquis. Knighton killed Ruth for the ruby, aided by Mason, whose story about a man in the compartment was manufactured to misdirect the inquiry. Knighton is exposed, Derek is cleared, and Katherine emerges from the case with the prospect of a life with Derek rather than the cautious isolation she expected.

recaps.text: American financier Rufus Van Aldin purchases the Heart of Fire, a celebrated ruby, and gives it to his daughter Ruth Kettering. Ruth is separated from her charming but penniless husband Derek, and Van Aldin urges her to complete the divorce. He is equally alarmed by her renewed connection with the Comte de la Roche, a polished adventurer who knows about the jewel. Van Aldin's trusted secretary, Major Richard Knighton, manages the arrangements. Elsewhere, Katherine Grey finishes years of service as companion to a difficult old woman and unexpectedly inherits a fortune. She decides to travel, entering a world in which her good sense is more reliable than her new money.

Katherine boards the Blue Train for the Riviera and falls into conversation with Ruth, who hints at an unhappy marriage and an important decision. In Paris Ruth dismisses her maid, Ada Mason, for the night. The next day Ruth is found dead in her compartment, her face badly injured and the Heart of Fire missing. Mason says a man was with Ruth in Paris but that she did not see him clearly. The known appointment with the Comte de la Roche immediately directs suspicion toward him. Derek Kettering has also been travelling in the region, and Ruth's death gives him a financial interest as her husband. Poirot, another passenger, agrees to help Van Aldin while the French authorities begin their inquiry.

At the Riviera Poirot compares the accounts of the train journey with the relationships surrounding Ruth. Katherine stays with her cousin Lady Rosalie Tamplin and Rosalie's sharp-eyed daughter Lenox, placing her near Derek and his lover Mirelle. Derek admits enough to look reckless but denies killing Ruth; Mirelle is jealous of the ease between him and Katherine. The count's interest in Ruth's jewels is real, yet Poirot doubts that his familiar form of fraud explains every feature of the murder. Mason's evidence remains central because it supplies the unknown man in Ruth's compartment, but her inability to identify him makes the story unusually convenient. Knighton assists Van Aldin and grows close to Katherine while Poirot quietly checks what each person knew about the ruby.

Poirot follows the jewel rather than the most visible romance. In Paris he consults Demetrius Papopolous, an old contact with detailed knowledge of stolen gems, and learns more about the international thief called the Marquis. The Heart of Fire is valuable enough to draw a professional scheme, and the mutilation of Ruth's face may have been meant to confuse identification as well as to show violence. The count can be tied to an attempt to profit from Ruth, but evidence against him does not account cleanly for the timing aboard the train. Poirot also studies Mason's prepared recollection, Derek's movements, Mirelle's changing statements, and the access enjoyed by people in Van Aldin's confidence. Katherine remains important because Ruth spoke to her without knowing her and because Katherine notices character without trying to build a case.

The inquiry narrows as Poirot separates several genuine deceptions from the murder itself. The Comte de la Roche has lied and schemed for the ruby, but his dishonesty is too obvious to settle the case. Mirelle tries to use what she knows of Derek's movements to keep control of him, while Derek's feelings for Katherine become harder to disguise. Poirot returns repeatedly to the information available before the journey: who knew Van Aldin had bought the Heart of Fire, who knew Ruth would carry it, and who could arrange testimony inside the sleeping car. Papopolous's information about the Marquis suggests that the robbery was not an impulsive act. Poirot applies pressure to the witness whose account created the apparent stranger in Ruth's compartment and prepares to confront the person behind it.

Poirot exposes Major Richard Knighton as Ruth Kettering's murderer and as the master jewel thief known as the Marquis. Knighton's place beside Van Aldin gave him advance knowledge of the Heart of Fire and Ruth's journey. Ada Mason was his accomplice, and her report of an indistinct man in Ruth's compartment was constructed to direct attention toward the Comte de la Roche while remaining flexible enough to survive questioning. Knighton killed Ruth aboard the train and stole the ruby, using the count's plans, Derek's financial interest, and Mirelle's jealousy as layers of misdirection. Poirot's inquiries through Papopolous connect the professional theft to the supposedly respectable secretary, and Mason's story fails under pressure. The ruby is recovered, Derek is cleared, and Knighton's interest in Katherine is stripped of its reassuring appearance. Katherine comes through the case independently wealthy and emotionally changed, with Derek now free and the possibility of a future between them.
